content:
Hiro Tanaka: Want to re-open the idea of freezing kernel autotune params on the 1.18 LTS line. Right now runtime does a lightweight autotune on first load for a few hot kernels and we’re seeing measurable variance across hosts/runs.

Hiro Tanaka: Proposal: pin the selected configs (tile sizes/num_warps/split-k etc) for LTS so the runtime is deterministic. Still allow override via env var for emergency perf issues.

Marcus Reed: +1 on determinism for LTS. Perf-canary has been noisy and a decent chunk is from autotune picking different winners depending on warmup / clock state.

Claire Dubois: Which kernels are we talking about exactly? attention fwd/bwd? kv cache ops? GEMM wrappers? I want to make sure we don’t accidentally freeze something that’s actually workload-dependent.

Hiro Tanaka: Targeting the ones we currently “fast autotune” at startup:
- prefill attention (flash-attn path)
- decode attention kernel variant selection
- KV cache compaction / memcpy-ish kernels
- a couple of fused MLP variants

Hiro Tanaka: Not proposing freezing anything that’s truly dynamic based on seq_len, just the *autotune* knobs that choose among a small set of static launch configs.

Jonas Weber: What’s the data on variance? If we’re going to lock this down for 12+ months we need numbers + guardrails.

Marcus Reed: I pulled a quick look from the LTS baseline runs (same commit, rerun 10x on same A100 host). With autotune on, p95 tok/s varied ~±4–6% depending on run order (esp first run after driver reset). With forced configs it’s within ±1.2%.

Marcus Reed: Similar story on H100 but smaller amplitude (±3% down to ±0.8%).

Allison Grant: From observability side, we’ve also seen “mystery” latency shifts after node replacements in Dedicated. Not huge, but enough to trigger customer questions when they compare before/after.

Noah Patel: I’m generally supportive but want to be careful: freezing can lock in a suboptimal choice for certain GPU SKUs or driver combos. How do we pick the pinned configs? Per-GPU? One-size-fits-all?

Hiro Tanaka: Suggest pinned table keyed by (kernel, arch, GPU SKU). Ex: sm80 A100 vs sm90 H100, and maybe L4 if we care. We already branch by arch in code; adding SKU-level entries is straightforward.

Claire Dubois: SKU-level might be too fine if customers have “A100 40GB vs 80GB” etc. But arch-level alone might be too coarse.

Jonas Weber: For LTS I’d rather keep the key small and explicit. Maybe (arch, memory bandwidth class) is overthinking. SKU list that we actually support in Dedicated/Private seems fine.

Connor O'Brien: From release engineering POV: freezing configs helps reproducibility and supports the “auditable artifact” story. But we need a clear escape hatch + documentation. If a customer’s workload regresses we can’t tell them “sorry, tune your own kernel.”

Connor O'Brien: Can we gate with:
1) default pinned
2) env var to re-enable autotune or set “unfrozen”
3) release notes callout + known issues entry if needed

Hiro Tanaka: Yep. Something like:
- `RUNTIME_KERNEL_AUTOTUNE=0` (default on LTS)
- `RUNTIME_KERNEL_AUTOTUNE=1` to restore prior behavior
- `RUNTIME_KERNEL_CONFIG_PROFILE=lts-pinned-v1` (optional, mostly for debugging)

Samir Qureshi: Concern: if we disable autotune on LTS but keep it on main, we’re splitting behavior. That’s ok but means backports touching kernels need extra care. Tests should cover both modes.

Hiro Tanaka: Agree. For LTS we only care pinned mode, but we should keep the code path healthy. We can run one CI job with autotune enabled as a smoke check.

Sofia Ivanova: Scheduling angle: anything that changes per-node kernel performance will show up as more/less batching efficiency. Pinning should make scheduler behavior more predictable across a fleet (good), but if pinned config lowers throughput we might need to revisit some queue/backpressure thresholds.

Marcus Reed: On throughput deltas: pinned configs are basically “median winner.” On A100, forced config is within ~1% of best autotune winner on our canonical workloads. Worst-case I saw was -2.3% on a very short prompt distribution.

Claire Dubois: That’s acceptable for LTS if we call it out. Also: make sure pinned configs are chosen under stable clocks (nvidia-smi -lgc) or at least multiple runs. Otherwise we’re pinning noise.

Marcus Reed: +1. I can rerun selection with fixed clocks and publish the table we’ll embed.

Allison Grant: Rollout: can we stage this behind a runtime flag and roll to one Dedicated cluster first? We’ll see if customer traffic has any weird p95 changes.

Connor O'Brien: For LTS branch, I’d prefer shipping pinned-by-default from day 1. But we can do staged rollout in Hosted/Dedicated before cutting the first patch. For Private, customers will get it when they opt into 1.18.x-lts.

Noah Patel: Another angle: do we freeze *autotune cache* too? Sometimes we persist results on disk and they get reused. That can also create “sticky” behavior across upgrades.

Hiro Tanaka: Good catch. For LTS, I propose we ignore any persisted cache and use the baked-in table. (Otherwise we defeat the point.)

Samir Qureshi: :thumbsup: Also reduces “why did it change after upgrade” tickets.

Jonas Weber: What about new GPU SKUs? If we add, say, B200 later, LTS pinned table won’t have entries.

Hiro Tanaka: For unknown GPUs on LTS:
- default to arch-level pinned if available
- else fall back to autotune (with a warning log + metric)

Hiro Tanaka: That way we’re deterministic for the common cases but not dead in the water.

Connor O'Brien: Please add a loud log line for fallback, and something we can put in release notes / support playbook: “If you’re on an unsupported GPU, LTS will autotune and performance may vary.”

Claire Dubois: I’d like the pinned table to be generated by a script checked into repo, not manually edited. Otherwise it’s going to drift.

Marcus Reed: I can add a small tool that runs perf harness + emits JSON mapping. Then we commit the generated file in the LTS branch. (Not at runtime.)

Hiro Tanaka: Works. We’ll treat the generated table as source-controlled artifact, and include the commit hash of the generation run.

Allison Grant: Any monitoring we want? If we’re trying to reduce variance, let’s measure it. Maybe metric like `kernel_config_source={pinned,autotune,fallback}` and a dashboard.

Sofia Ivanova: +1. Also correlate with scheduler metrics (queue wait, batch size distribution). If throughput drops slightly, scheduler may compensate by batching more.

Connor O'Brien: Action items:
- Hiro: draft PR on LTS branch to default to pinned configs and ignore autotune cache
- Marcus/Claire: rerun selection under fixed clocks, produce pinned table for A100/H100/L4 (whatever’s in scope)
- Allison: add metric + quick dashboard panel for config source
- Connor: update LTS release notes template to mention “Kernel autotune frozen for determinism” + escape hatch

Hiro Tanaka: I’ll open PR today. Will tag it `lts` + `perf` and add a short doc snippet. :shipit:

Marcus Reed: I’ll start the reruns now. Expect results EOD tomorrow.

Claire Dubois: Please include raw benchmark notes somewhere (even just in the PR description): which driver, clocks, warmup, number of trials.

Jonas Weber: If we see any regression >3% on canonical workloads, I want a review before we merge. Otherwise I’m good.

Hiro Tanaka: Deal. I’ll post numbers in thread once Marcus shares.

Connor O'Brien: Also reminder: anything touching kernel behavior needs a note in the LTS known issues doc if there’s a risk tradeoff (even “slight throughput tradeoff for determinism”).

Samir Qureshi: +1. And add a one-liner in troubleshooting: “If you suspect pinned config is hurting perf, set env var and compare.”

Allison Grant: Thanks all. This will help a lot with the “node replacement changed my latency” conversations.
